questions.question: Serial communication / serial port / serial modes. UART working and features.
questions.answer_html:
Serial Communication & UART

Serial communication is the process of transmitting data one single bit at a time sequentially over a single communication line or wire. A UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) is a hardware circuit that converts parallel data from the CPU into serial bits for transmission, and vice versa.

1. Serial vs. Parallel Communication

  • Parallel: Sends an entire byte (8 bits) simultaneously across 8 separate parallel wires. Fast for very short distances (e.g., inside a chip), but expensive and suffers from crosstalk and clock skew over long wires.
  • Serial: Sends bits sequentially across 1 or 2 wires. Requires fewer pins, cheaper cables, and transmits reliably over long distances.

2. Asynchronous vs. Synchronous Serial Data Transmission

  • Synchronous: Sender and receiver share a dedicated clock wire. Data bits are synchronized to clock pulses (e.g., SPI, I2C).
  • Asynchronous (UART): No shared clock line! Sender and receiver are configured to the exact same Baud Rate (bits per second). Special Start and Stop framing bits are added to synchronize byte reception.

3. UART Frame Format

Every asynchronous character transmitted by UART is wrapped inside a Frame:

  1. Idle State: When no data is being sent, the line stays at Logic HIGH (Mark condition).
  2. Start Bit (1 bit): The line drops to Logic LOW for 1 bit period, notifying the receiver that a new byte is starting.
  3. Data Bits (5 to 8 bits): The actual information bits, transmitted Least Significant Bit (LSB) first.
  4. Parity Bit (Optional, 1 bit): Used for simple error detection (Even or Odd parity).
  5. Stop Bit(s) (1 or 2 bits): The line returns to Logic HIGH to signal the end of the frame and allow receiver clock recovery.

4. 8051 Serial Port Modes (Controlled by SCON Register)

Mode SM0 SM1 Description & Frame Size Baud Rate Source
Mode 0 0 0 8-bit Shift Register (half-duplex) Fixed: $f_{osc} / 12$ (1 MHz at 12 MHz crystal)
Mode 1 0 1 Standard 8-bit UART (10-bit frame: 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop) Variable: Set by Timer 1 overflow rate (Most Common)
Mode 2 1 0 9-bit UART (11-bit frame: 1 start + 8 data + 1 programmable 9th bit + 1 stop) Fixed: $f_{osc} / 32$ or $f_{osc} / 64$ (set by SMOD bit)
Mode 3 1 1 9-bit UART (11-bit frame with 9th bit for multiprocessor communication) Variable: Set by Timer 1 overflow rate

5. Key 8051 Serial Registers

  • SBUF (Serial Buffer — Address 0x99): Two physically separate registers sharing one address. Writing to SBUF loads the transmit buffer; reading from SBUF reads the receive buffer.
  • SCON (Serial Control — Address 0x98):
    • SM0, SM1: Selects Serial Mode (Mode 1: SM0=0, SM1=1).
    • REN (Receive Enable): Set to 1 to allow UART to receive incoming bytes.
    • TI (Transmit Interrupt Flag): Set to 1 by hardware when a byte finishes transmitting. Must be cleared by software!
    • RI (Receive Interrupt Flag): Set to 1 by hardware when a complete byte is received in SBUF. Must be cleared by software!
  • PCON (Power Control Register): Bit 7 (SMOD) when set to 1 doubles the baud rate.

questions.question: Program to transfer a message serially at a given baud rate.
questions.answer_html:
8051 Serial Transmission Program

To transmit characters serially via the 8051 UART, Timer 1 is configured in Mode 2 (8-bit auto-reload) to generate the standard baud rate clock (e.g., 9600 baud using an 11.0592 MHz crystal).

1. Step-by-Step Configuration Sequence

  1. Configure TMOD = 0x20 (Timer 1 in Mode 2: 8-bit auto-reload).
  2. Load TH1 = 0xFD ($-3$) to set baud rate to 9600 baud with 11.0592 MHz crystal.
  3. Configure SCON = 0x50 (Mode 1: 8-bit UART, 1 stop bit, Receiver Enabled REN=1).
  4. Start Timer 1 by setting TR1 = 1.
  5. Load the ASCII character into SBUF.
  6. Monitor the Transmit Interrupt flag TI in a loop until it becomes 1 (hardware sets TI=1 when byte transmission finishes).
  7. Clear TI = 0 so the next character can be sent.

2. C Program (Keil C51)

#include <reg51.h>

// Function to initialize UART at 9600 baud
void UART_Init(void) {
    TMOD = 0x20;   // Timer 1, Mode 2 (8-bit auto-reload)
    TH1  = 0xFD;   // 9600 baud at 11.0592 MHz
    SCON = 0x50;   // Mode 1 (8-bit UART), enable receiver
    TR1  = 1;      // Start Timer 1
}

// Function to transmit a single character
void UART_TxChar(char ch) {
    SBUF = ch;     // Load byte into transmit buffer
    while (TI == 0); // Wait until transmission is complete
    TI = 0;        // Clear TI flag for next byte
}

// Function to transmit an entire string
void UART_TxString(char *str) {
    while (*str) {
        UART_TxChar(*str++);
    }
}

void main(void) {
    UART_Init();   // Initialize serial hardware
    
    while(1) {
        UART_TxString("HELLO EMBEDDED SYSTEM\r\n");
        // Delay between repeated transmissions
        for (unsigned int i = 0; i < 30000; i++);
    }
}

3. Equivalent 8051 Assembly Language Program

        ORG 0000H
        MOV TMOD, #20H     ; Timer 1, Mode 2 (8-bit auto-reload)
        MOV TH1, #-3       ; 9600 Baud (FDH)
        MOV SCON, #50H     ; Mode 1, 8-bit UART, REN enabled
        SETB TR1           ; Start Timer 1

AGAIN:  MOV DPTR, #MYDATA  ; Point to start of string
NEXT:   CLR A
        MOVC A, @A+DPTR    ; Get character from ROM
        JZ AGAIN           ; If null terminator (0), repeat
        ACALL SEND_CHAR    ; Transmit character
        INC DPTR           ; Point to next character
        SJMP NEXT

SEND_CHAR:
        MOV SBUF, A        ; Load character into SBUF
WAIT_TX:
        JNB TI, WAIT_TX    ; Wait until TI flag = 1
        CLR TI             ; Clear TI flag
        RET

MYDATA: DB "HELLO EMBEDDED SYSTEM", 0DH, 0AH, 0
        END

questions.question: Find TH1 value for a given baud rate.
questions.answer_html:
Derivation of TH1 Register Value for 8051 Baud Rates

In 8051 serial Mode 1, the baud rate is determined by the overflow rate of Timer 1 in Mode 2 (8-bit auto-reload). The value placed in register TH1 sets the countdown period.

1. Why is an 11.0592 MHz Crystal Always Used in 8051 Serial Systems?

  1. The 8051 internal clock circuitry divides the crystal frequency ($f_{osc}$) by 12 to generate the machine cycle frequency:
    $$f_{\text{machine}} = \frac{11.0592\text{ MHz}}{12} = 921,600\text{ Hz}$$
  2. The 8051 UART hardware frequency divider divides this by another 32 (when SMOD = 0):
    $$f_{\text{UART}} = \frac{921,600\text{ Hz}}{32} = 28,800\text{ Hz}$$
  3. The Key Reason: The number 28,800 divides evenly by all standard commercial baud rates without any fractional remainder!
    • $28,800 / 9600 = 3$ (Exact integer!)
    • $28,800 / 4800 = 6$ (Exact integer!)
    • $28,800 / 2400 = 12$ (Exact integer!)
    • $28,800 / 1200 = 24$ (Exact integer!)
    Contrast with 12 MHz crystal: $\frac{12\text{ MHz}}{12 \times 32} = 31,250\text{ Hz}$. Then $31,250 / 9600 = 3.255$, which has an 8.5% timing error that causes garbled characters!

2. The General Mathematical Formula for TH1

$$\text{Baud Rate} = \frac{2^{\text{SMOD}}}{32} \times \frac{f_{osc}}{12 \times (256 - \text{TH1})}$$

Assuming standard SMOD = 0 ($2^0 = 1$) and $f_{osc} = 11.0592\text{ MHz}$:

$$(256 - \text{TH1}) = \frac{11,059,200}{384 \times \text{Baud Rate}} = \frac{28,800}{\text{Baud Rate}}$$

3. Step-by-Step Calculation for Standard Baud Rates

A. For 9600 Baud:

  1. $256 - \text{TH1} = \frac{28,800}{9600} = 3$
  2. $\text{TH1} = 256 - 3 = 253$
  3. Convert 253 to Hexadecimal: $253_{10} = \mathbf{0xFD}$ (or $-3$)

B. For 4800 Baud:

  1. $256 - \text{TH1} = \frac{28,800}{4800} = 6$
  2. $\text{TH1} = 256 - 6 = 250$
  3. Convert 250 to Hexadecimal: $250_{10} = \mathbf{0xFA}$ (or $-6$)

C. For 2400 Baud:

  1. $256 - \text{TH1} = \frac{28,800}{2400} = 12$
  2. $\text{TH1} = 256 - 12 = 244$
  3. Convert 244 to Hexadecimal: $244_{10} = \mathbf{0xF4}$ (or $-12$)

D. For 1200 Baud:

  1. $256 - \text{TH1} = \frac{28,800}{1200} = 24$
  2. $\text{TH1} = 256 - 24 = 232$
  3. Convert 232 to Hexadecimal: $232_{10} = \mathbf{0xE8}$ (or $-24$)

4. Summary Table of TH1 Values (at 11.0592 MHz, SMOD=0)

Baud Rate Division Factor $(256 - \text{TH1})$ Decimal TH1 Value Hexadecimal TH1 Value
9600 3 253 0xFD ($-3$)
4800 6 250 0xFA ($-6$)
2400 12 244 0xF4 ($-12$)
1200 24 232 0xE8 ($-24$)

questions.question: Working of the I2C protocol with diagram.
questions.answer_html:
I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) Protocol

I2C is a synchronous, bidirectional, half-duplex, multi-master, multi-slave serial bus developed by Philips (NXP). It allows microcontrollers to communicate with multiple peripheral chips (EEPROM, RTC, sensors) using only two physical wires.

1. Bus Hardware Topology Diagram

2. The Two Bus Lines & Pull-Up Resistors

  • SDA (Serial Data): Bidirectional line for carrying data and address bits.
  • SCL (Serial Clock): Clock line generated by the Master to synchronize data transfer.
  • Open-Drain / Open-Collector Design: All devices connect to the bus with open-drain pins. Pull-up resistors (typically 4.7 kΩ) pull the lines up to +Vdd when idle. Any device can safely pull the line LOW to GND without causing short-circuit contention (wired-AND logic).

3. Key Protocol Events & Bus Conditions

  1. Idle State: Both SDA and SCL are pulled HIGH by the pull-up resistors.
  2. START Condition (S): Initiated by the Master. The SDA line transitions from HIGH to LOW while SCL remains HIGH.
  3. Data Validity Rule: Data on SDA must remain stable during the entire HIGH period of the SCL clock pulse. SDA can change state only when SCL is LOW.
  4. Acknowledge (ACK / NACK): Every 8-bit byte transferred is followed by a 9th clock pulse for confirmation:
    • ACK (Acknowledge): Receiver pulls SDA LOW during the 9th SCL pulse (byte successfully received).
    • NACK (Not Acknowledge): Receiver leaves SDA HIGH during the 9th pulse (signals error or end of transfer).
  5. STOP Condition (P): Terminated by the Master. The SDA line transitions from LOW to HIGH while SCL remains HIGH.

4. Complete I2C Transmission Frame Sequence

$$\text{[START]} \rightarrow [\text{7-bit Slave Address} + \text{R/W bit}] \rightarrow [\text{ACK}] \rightarrow [\text{8-bit Data/Register Byte}] \rightarrow [\text{ACK}] \rightarrow [\text{STOP}]$$

5. Speed Modes and Characteristics

  • Standard Mode (Sm): Up to 100 kbps.
  • Fast Mode (Fm): Up to 400 kbps.
  • Fast Mode Plus (Fm+): Up to 1 Mbps.
  • High-Speed Mode (Hs): Up to 3.4 Mbps.
  • Addressing: Standard 7-bit addressing supports up to 128 unique devices on the same two wires (10-bit addressing is also supported).

questions.question: CAN bus communication with diagram, and its application.
questions.answer_html:
CAN (Controller Area Network) Protocol

CAN bus is a robust, message-based, multi-master broadcast serial network protocol developed by Robert Bosch for the automotive industry. It allows automotive Electronic Control Units (ECUs) to communicate without a central host computer.

1. CAN Bus Architecture and Differential Signaling

2. Physical Layer: Differential Signaling

CAN transmits data over a twisted-pair cable using differential voltage signaling to provide immunity against electromagnetic noise:

Logic State CAN_H Line CAN_L Line Differential Voltage $(V_{\text{diff}} = V_H - V_L)$ Bus Priority
Dominant (Logic 0) Driven to 3.5V Driven to 1.5V $+2.0\text{ V}$ Highest: Overwrites Recessive!
Recessive (Logic 1) Biased to 2.5V Biased to 2.5V $0.0\text{ V}$ Lowest: Passive state

Bus Termination: A 120 Ω termination resistor is placed at each physical end of the twisted pair to eliminate high-frequency signal reflections.

3. Key Protocol Mechanisms

  1. Non-Destructive Bitwise Arbitration: When multiple nodes start transmitting at the same instant, they compare their message identifiers bit-by-bit. Because a Dominant bit (0) overwrites a Recessive bit (1), the node with the lowest numeric ID wins the bus and continues transmitting with zero delay or data corruption!
  2. Message-Based Addressing: Nodes do not have physical network addresses. Instead, messages carry an 11-bit Identifier (or 29-bit in CAN 2.0B) that describes the content and sets its priority (e.g., ID 0x010 for ABS braking has higher priority than ID 0x350 for air conditioning).
  3. Comprehensive Error Handling: Features 15-bit CRC checksum, bit stuffing, frame checks, and automatic message retransmission upon error.

4. CAN Data Frame Fields

  • SOF (Start of Frame — 1 bit): Single dominant bit (0).
  • Identifier (11 bits): Priority and message tag.
  • RTR (Remote Transmission Request — 1 bit): 0 for data frame, 1 for remote request.
  • Control / DLC (6 bits): Data Length Code (specifies payload from 0 to 8 bytes).
  • Data Field (0 to 8 bytes): Actual payload data.
  • CRC (15 bits): Checksum for error verification.
  • ACK (2 bits): Transmitting node sends recessive; receiving nodes overwrite with dominant.
  • EOF (End of Frame — 7 bits): 7 recessive bits.

5. Real-World Applications of CAN Bus

  • Automotive Systems: Connects engine management, ABS, airbags, transmission, dashboard, and power steering.
  • Commercial Vehicles & Heavy Machinery: Construction equipment, tractors (SAE J1939 standard).
  • Avionics & Aerospace: Flight control subsystems (CANaerospace).
  • Industrial Automation: Factory robotics and conveyor network protocols (DeviceNet, CANopen).

questions.question: SPI protocol, and comparison of UART, SPI, I2C and CAN.
questions.answer_html:
SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) Protocol

SPI is a high-speed, synchronous, full-duplex, master-slave serial interface bus developed by Motorola. It is used for short-distance board-level communication between a microcontroller and fast peripherals like SD cards, displays, and ADCs.

1. SPI 4-Wire Hardware Topology

  1. MOSI (Master Out Slave In): Data line driven by Master to send data to the Slave.
  2. MISO (Master In Slave Out): Data line driven by Slave to send data back to the Master.
  3. SCK (Serial Clock): Clock pulses generated by the Master to synchronize bit transfers.
  4. $\overline{ ext{SS}}$ or $\overline{ ext{CS}}$ (Slave Select / Chip Select): Dedicated active-LOW line for each slave. When the Master pulls $\overline{ ext{SS}}$ LOW, that specific slave is selected for communication.

2. Clock Polarity (CPOL) and Clock Phase (CPHA) Modes

SPI features 4 operational modes configured by two register bits:

  • CPOL (Clock Polarity): 0 = Clock is idle LOW; 1 = Clock is idle HIGH.
  • CPHA (Clock Phase): 0 = Data sampled on first clock edge; 1 = Data sampled on second clock edge.
  • Mode 0 (CPOL=0, CPHA=0) is the most popular mode used by SD cards and sensors.

3. Comprehensive Comparison Table: UART, SPI, I2C, and CAN

Parameter UART SPI I2C CAN
Synchronization Asynchronous (No clock line) Synchronous (SCK line) Synchronous (SCL line) Asynchronous (Bit stuffing)
Wire Count 2 wires (Tx, Rx) 4 wires (MOSI, MISO, SCK, SS) 2 wires (SDA, SCL) 2 wires (CAN_H, CAN_L)
Duplex Mode Full-Duplex Full-Duplex Half-Duplex Half-Duplex
Bus Topology Point-to-Point (1 to 1) Master – Multi-Slave (Dedicated SS lines) Multi-Master – Multi-Slave (Address based) Multi-Master Broadcast (Message ID based)
Data Speed Up to 115.2 kbps (can reach ~1 Mbps) Fastest: 10 to 50+ Mbps 100 kbps to 3.4 Mbps 1 Mbps (CAN 2.0) to 5 Mbps (CAN-FD)
Distance Short to Moderate (~15 m with RS-232) Short (< 30 cm on same PCB) Short (< 2 m on same PCB) Longest (Up to 1 km at 50 kbps; 40m at 1 Mbps)
Error Detection Optional simple 1-bit Parity None (built-in) ACK / NACK bit only Robust 15-bit CRC, ACK, Frame checks
Best Application PC debugging, GPS, Bluetooth modems SD cards, graphical TFT LCDs, fast ADCs On-board sensors, RTC clocks, EEPROM Automotive engine/brake control, avionics

questions.question: Compare USB 2.0, Bluetooth, Zigbee and RFID with respect to features and applications.
questions.answer_html:
Peripheral & Wireless Communication Technologies

Embedded devices connect to local host computers and distributed wireless IoT networks using standard protocols: USB 2.0 (wired), Bluetooth (short-range wireless), Zigbee (low-power mesh), and RFID (contactless identification).

1. Overview of the Four Technologies

  1. USB 2.0 (Universal Serial Bus): A 4-wire wired peripheral interface ($V_{BUS}$, $D+$, $D-$, $GND$) using differential NRZI signaling. Operates in a Tiered Star topology managed by a single Host controller.
  2. Bluetooth (Classic & BLE): A 2.4 GHz ISM band wireless protocol designed for short-range cable replacement (WPAN) between portable consumer devices. Uses Frequency Hopping Spread Spectrum (FHSS) across 79 channels.
  3. Zigbee (IEEE 802.15.4): A low-power, low-data-rate 2.4 GHz wireless protocol designed specifically for industrial sensing and home automation. Features self-healing Mesh networking supporting over 65,000 nodes!
  4. RFID (Radio Frequency Identification): An automatic identification technology consisting of an RFID Reader and an RFID Tag (Transponder). Uses electromagnetic induction or backscatter coupling; passive tags require no battery!

2. Comprehensive Comparison Table

Feature USB 2.0 Bluetooth (v4.0 / BLE) Zigbee (802.15.4) RFID
Media Type Wired (4-wire shielded cable) Wireless (2.4 GHz RF) Wireless (2.4 GHz, 868/915 MHz RF) Wireless (LF, HF 13.56MHz, UHF)
Maximum Data Rate High Speed: 480 Mbps 1 to 3 Mbps (BLE: 1–2 Mbps) Low: 250 kbps Very Low: Up to 424 kbps
Operating Range Max 5 meters (cable length) 10 to 100 meters 10 to 100 meters (extended via mesh) Few cm (Passive) to 10m+ (Active)
Network Topology Tiered Star (Host / Device) Piconet / Scatternet (Star) Mesh, Star, Cluster Tree Point-to-Point (Interrogator – Tag)
Power Consumption High (supplied by host bus 500mA) Very Low (BLE: runs on coin cell) Lowest (Batteries last 2–5 years) Zero for Passive Tags (powered by RF field)
Max Network Nodes Up to 127 devices per host 8 active devices per Piconet Up to 65,535 nodes One tag scanned at a time (anti-collision)
Typical Applications PC mouse, keyboard, flash drives, cameras. Wireless headphones, smartwatches, heart rate monitors. Smart home lighting, industrial wireless sensor networks. Access cards, toll plazas (FASTag), inventory tracking.
